name: Optical bistability and the Ikeda route to chaos
summary: A cavity filled with a Kerr medium has an S-shaped transmission curve bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations, which gives hysteresis and optical switching. Ikeda showed that the delayed ring-cavity map period-doubles into chaos as the input power rises, a Feigenbaum cascade realized in optics.
sources: Feigenbaum (1978). "Quantitative universality for a class of nonlinear transformations". *J. Stat. Phys.* 19, 25. [doi:10.1007/BF01020332](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332)

name: Lorenz–Haken: single-mode laser equals Lorenz system
summary: Haken (1975) showed that the Maxwell–Bloch equations of a homogeneously broadened single-mode laser (field, polarization, inversion) are isomorphic to Lorenz's convection model. A bad-cavity laser pumped far above threshold therefore shows Lorenz chaos, which has been observed in far-infrared NH3 lasers. Class-B lasers reach chaos when modulation or delayed feedback is added.
breaks: Lorenz chaos needs the bad-cavity condition σ>b+1 and pumping many times above threshold, which ordinary lasers never reach. For convection the three-mode equations are a severe truncation, while for the laser they are close to exact.

name: Ray chaos in deformed optical microcavities
summary: Rays in a dielectric microdisk follow billiard orbits. Deforming the circle breaks the KAM tori, and whispering-gallery rays then diffuse chaotically in the Poincaré surface of section until they drop below the critical angle and refract out. This explains the directional emission and spoiled Q of asymmetric-resonant-cavity lasers.
breaks: When kR is not large, wave effects such as dynamical tunnelling and scarred modes modify the ray picture.

name: Optical fibres as a testbed for NLS rogue waves
summary: Deep-water wave groups and fibre pulses both obey the focusing NLS. Benjamin–Feir modulational instability, Akhmediev breathers and the Peregrine soliton, all proposed prototypes of rogue waves, have therefore been generated in optical fibres and water tanks with the same normalized solutions. Optical rogue waves also appear in supercontinuum generation.
breaks: Ocean waves add higher-order (Dysthe) corrections, directional spreading and breaking, so it is contested whether real rogue waves are NLS breathers rather than linear focusing. Fibres add Raman effects and higher-order dispersion.

name: Optical solitons from the integrable NLS equation
summary: A pulse envelope in a Kerr fibre with anomalous dispersion obeys the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which inverse scattering solves exactly. Self-phase modulation balances group-velocity dispersion, and the fundamental sech soliton (N=1) and the higher-order breathers are the same objects found in deep-water wave groups.
breaks: Real fibres add loss, the Raman self-frequency shift and higher-order dispersion, all of which break integrability. Solitons then shed dispersive waves and undergo fission, which is what drives supercontinuum generation.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

Gardner, Greene, Kruskal & Miura (1967). "Method for Solving the Korteweg-deVries Equation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1095. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095)

name: Lugiato–Lefever patterns and Kerr microcombs
summary: A continuously driven Kerr microresonator obeys the Lugiato–Lefever equation, a damped and driven NLS first derived for transverse optical patterns. Its Turing instability creates the primary comb (Turing rolls). Coexistence of homogeneous and localized states yields dissipative Kerr solitons, which are the mode-locked microcombs.
sources: Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Injection locking of lasers follows the Adler equation
summary: A slave laser injected with weak light from a master laser phase-locks when the detuning lies inside the locking range. It follows the Adler equation of phase synchronization, the same one that describes Huygens clocks and Kuramoto oscillators. Coupled laser arrays show Kuramoto-type synchronization transitions, and mode-locking is the phase locking of many cavity modes.
breaks: In semiconductor lasers, the linewidth-enhancement factor couples amplitude to phase. This skews the locking range and can cause instabilities that the pure phase model does not capture.
sources: Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Cavity modes and LC lines as mechanical oscillators
summary: Each normal mode of a resonant cavity obeys a damped driven oscillator equation, with the quality factor Q=ω0/Δω defined exactly as for a mechanical resonator. A lumped LC transmission line is a mass–spring chain (L↔m, 1/C↔k): it has the same discrete-lattice dispersion and cutoff, and its continuum limit is the same wave equation.
map: \ddot a+\frac{\omega_0}{Q}\dot a+\omega_0^2a=f(t);\ L\leftrightarrow m,\ C^{-1}\leftrightarrow k,\ R\leftrightarrow b;\ \omega(k)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{LC}}\left|\sin\frac{ka}{2}\right|
breaks: The analogy holds mode by mode, but not for the field's spatial structure. Cavity modes carry polarization and vector boundary conditions, and their density grows as ω², which a scalar chain does not reproduce.

name: Coupled-mode theory: directional couplers as coupled pendula
summary: Two evanescently coupled waveguides exchange power along z exactly as two weakly coupled identical pendula exchange energy in time (beats). Detuning gives incomplete transfer and an avoided crossing of the supermodes. Arrays of waveguides or ring resonators are oscillator chains, with tight-binding dispersion and discrete diffraction.
map: i\frac{da_{1,2}}{dz}=\beta a_{1,2}+\kappa a_{2,1}\ \Rightarrow\ P_2(z)=\sin^2\kappa z;\qquad \beta(k)=\beta_0+2\kappa\cos kd
breaks: Propagation distance plays the role of time. The coupled-mode equations are first order and Schrödinger-like, the rotating-wave limit of the second-order pendulum equations.

name: Fano lines and plasmon hybridization from coupled oscillators
summary: Two coupled damped oscillators, a broad bright mode driven by light and a narrow dark mode, produce an asymmetric Fano line with a transparency window. This is the standard classical model of plasmon-induced transparency in metamaterials. Coupled nanoparticle plasmons split into bonding and antibonding hybrid modes just as coupled pendula do.
map: \ddot x_1+\gamma_1\dot x_1+\omega_1^2x_1-\kappa x_2=\frac{F}{m}e^{-i\omega t},\quad \ddot x_2+\gamma_2\dot x_2+\omega_2^2x_2-\kappa x_1=0,\ \gamma_2\ll\gamma_1
breaks: In atomic EIT, the dark mode is a quantum superposition of ground states prepared by a control laser. The classical model reproduces the lineshape and dispersion, but not storage of a quantum state.

name: Topological bands of coupled resonators and spring lattices
summary: Topological photonics treats lattices of coupled resonators and waveguides as normal-mode problems whose bands carry winding or Chern numbers. Applying the same band topology to coupled pendula, gyroscope lattices and spring networks gives mechanical topological insulators and edge modes in isostatic lattices. SSH-chain edge states appear in both.
breaks: Mechanical lattices are second order in time (an ω² eigenproblem) and have no Fermi level, and modes protected by time reversal need engineered pseudospins. Robust one-way edge modes require broken time reversal, for example spinning gyroscopes or magneto-optic media.

name: Lorentz–Drude oscillator model of dielectric response
summary: Treating bound electrons as driven damped oscillators gives the Lorentz permittivity: normal dispersion below resonance, and absorption with anomalous dispersion at resonance. Setting the spring constant to zero gives the Drude metal with plasma frequency ωp. Causality of the oscillator's response yields the Kramers–Kronig relations.
breaks: The resonance frequencies and oscillator strengths f_j come from quantum transitions. The classical model gets the functional form right but cannot supply these parameters.

name: Split-ring and plasmon resonators as damped oscillators
summary: A split-ring resonator is an LC circuit. Its Lorentzian response gives an effective permeability that turns negative just above resonance, which is the route to negative-index media. A localized surface plasmon is a nanoparticle's conduction-electron cloud oscillating against the restoring field of its own surface charge; it resonates at the Fröhlich condition, at ωp/√3 for a Drude sphere in vacuum.
breaks: Plasmon damping includes Landau damping and surface scattering, and very small particles show quantum size effects. A single classical oscillator misses all of these.

name: Radiation reaction as oscillator damping
summary: A charged oscillator loses energy at the Larmor rate. For near-harmonic motion the Abraham–Lorentz force mτ0 d³x/dt³ reduces to a damping rate γ=ω0²τ0. This gives the classical natural linewidth Δλ=(4π/3)re≈1.2×10⁻¹⁴ m, independent of frequency.
breaks: Taken exactly, the third-order Abraham–Lorentz equation has runaway solutions and preacceleration, so it is used only perturbatively (the Landau–Lifshitz form). For atoms, quantum linewidths replace the classical value.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)

name: Rayleigh and Thomson scattering from a driven electron
summary: When light drives a bound electron, the scattering cross-section is the square of the oscillator's response. Far below resonance it rises as ω⁴ (Rayleigh scattering, the blue sky); far above, it tends to the frequency-independent Thomson value; near ω0 it shows a Lorentzian resonance peak.
breaks: At photon energies comparable to mc², Thomson scattering gives way to Compton scattering, with recoil and the Klein–Nishina cross-section, which the classical oscillator cannot produce.

name: Impedance, reflection and waveguide cutoff for sound and light
summary: For both sound and light, normal-incidence reflection follows from impedance mismatch: r=(Z2−Z1)/(Z2+Z1), with Z=ρc for sound and Z=√(μ/ε) for light. Quarter-wave matching layers on ultrasound transducers work like anti-reflection coatings. Acoustic ducts carry higher modes with cutoff frequencies and evanescent tails, as metal waveguides do.
breaks: Sound in a fluid is a scalar longitudinal wave. A rigid duct therefore carries a plane mode with no cutoff, which a hollow metal guide lacks because it has no TEM mode, and sound has no polarization or TE/TM split. Elastic solids add shear waves, and P–S mode conversion at interfaces.

name: Acoustic metamaterials and transformation acoustics
summary: Ideas from electromagnetic metamaterials carried over to sound. Locally resonant inclusions give negative effective mass density or bulk modulus, producing double-negative acoustic media, and phononic crystals mirror photonic band gaps. Because the 2D acoustic equations are form-invariant, Pendry-style transformation cloaks can be built for sound, with density playing the role of permeability and compressibility that of permittivity.
map: \rho\leftrightarrow\mu,\ \ K^{-1}\leftrightarrow\varepsilon\ \ (\text{2D, one polarization});\quad \rho_{eff}(\omega)<0\ \text{just above a local resonance}
breaks: Full elastodynamics, which includes shear waves, is not form-invariant under coordinate transformations, so elastic cloaks need exotic Willis-type media. Sound has no polarization, and acoustic metamaterials are often lossy and narrowband.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)

name: Brillouin scattering couples light to sound
summary: Light Bragg-reflects off an acoustic wave and is Doppler-shifted by the sound frequency. At high intensity, electrostriction drives the acoustic wave itself, giving stimulated Brillouin scattering. For narrow-linewidth light this is the lowest-threshold fibre nonlinearity, with a shift of about 11 GHz in silica at 1550 nm, and it is used in Brillouin lasers, slow light and distributed strain sensing.

name: Mach cone and Cherenkov cone
summary: A source that outruns the waves it emits builds a conical wavefront from the Huygens envelope. A supersonic body gives the Mach cone, and a charge moving faster than c/n gives the Cherenkov cone. The geometry is the same once c_s is replaced by c/n.
breaks: Cherenkov light is linear radiation from a charge in a dispersive dielectric. It is emitted only at frequencies where n(ω)>1/β, with a Frank–Tamm spectrum proportional to ω. A sonic boom is instead a nonlinear shock (an N-wave) from a body displacing fluid.

name: Paul traps evade Earnshaw by Mathieu stabilization
summary: Earnshaw's theorem, which says Laplace's equation allows no potential minimum, forbids trapping charges with static electric fields. An rf quadrupole makes each coordinate obey a Mathieu equation whose stability region gives dynamic confinement. This Kapitza-pendulum mechanism is behind ion traps and quadrupole mass filters.

name: Laser as a Van der Pol self-sustained oscillator
summary: Semiclassically, the single-mode laser field is a Van der Pol oscillator. Gain acts as negative damping, threshold is a Hopf bifurcation, and gain saturation fixes a limit-cycle amplitude while leaving the phase free. The output is a self-sustained oscillator whose phase diffusion sets the Schawlow–Townes linewidth.
map: \ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0\ \leftrightarrow\ \dot{\mathcal E}=\tfrac12(G-\kappa)\mathcal E-\beta|\mathcal E|^2\mathcal E
breaks: The phase diffusion that sets the linewidth is driven by spontaneous emission, a quantum noise source that the deterministic Van der Pol equation does not contain. Multimode and class-B lasers add relaxation oscillations and mode competition.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Anharmonic electron oscillator model of χ(2) and χ(3)
summary: Adding quadratic and cubic terms to the Lorentz oscillator produces harmonics and an intensity-dependent response. An asymmetric x² restoring force gives χ(2), which vanishes for centrosymmetric potentials. A Duffing x³ term gives χ(3): the Kerr index n2 (an amplitude-dependent frequency) and third-harmonic generation. The model also yields Miller's rule.
breaks: Real nonlinear susceptibilities come from quantum transition matrix elements. They also have non-electronic sources (Raman, orientational, thermal) that a single oscillator leaves out.
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)

name: Optical parametric amplification as parametric resonance
summary: A pump wave modulating a χ(2) medium amplifies a signal and an idler with ωs+ωi=ωp. The degenerate case ωs=ωp/2 is the parametric resonance of a swing pumped at twice its natural frequency. It shares the phase-sensitive gain (one quadrature amplified, the other deamplified) and exponential growth above threshold, and the OPO is its self-oscillating form.
breaks: Optical parametric gain needs phase matching across a propagating medium, a spatial condition that a single swing has no counterpart for. The non-degenerate case couples two distinct modes.

name: Kapitza effective potential is the ponderomotive energy
summary: Averaging motion in a rapidly oscillating force F0 cos ωt gives Kapitza's effective potential F0²/4mω². For an electron in a laser field this is the ponderomotive energy Up. It sets the strong-field scales of attosecond physics, including the high-harmonic cutoff Ip+3.17Up, and it pushes electrons out of intense foci.
breaks: The averaging requires the field to vary slowly in space over one quiver excursion. At relativistic intensities (a0≳1), magnetic forces and the relativistic mass increase modify Up.
sources: Krausz & Ivanov (2009). "Attosecond physics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 163. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163)

name: Sagnac interferometers as optical gyroscopes
summary: Beams sent both ways around a loop rotating at Ω pick up a phase difference proportional to the enclosed area, which gives an absolute measurement of rotation. Ring-laser and fibre-optic gyroscopes built on this effect have largely replaced spinning-rotor gyroscopes in inertial navigation. Large ring lasers resolve Earth's rotation.
breaks: The optical device has no angular momentum. It senses rotation through the light travel time in the rotating frame, not through gyroscopic rigidity, so it shows no precession or nutation and needs no spin-up.

name: Larmor precession of magnetic moments as a gyroscope
summary: A magnetic dipole tied to angular momentum, μ=γL, feels the torque μ×B and precesses about B at ωL=γB. This is the same equation that makes a heavy top precess under the torque of gravity. The gyroscopic picture underlies NMR, ESR and MRI.
map: \frac{d\mathbf L}{dt}=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B=-\gamma\mathbf B\times\mathbf L\ \leftrightarrow\ \frac{d\mathbf L}{dt}=\mathbf r\times m\mathbf g;\quad \omega_L=\gamma B,\ \Omega_{top}=\frac{mgr}{L}
breaks: The magnetic torque scales with L, so the Larmor frequency does not depend on the size of the spin; a top, by contrast, precesses more slowly the faster it spins. The top's steady precession is also only the fast-spin approximation, with nutation added on top.

name: Quadrupole moment is the traceless inertia tensor
summary: For a mass distribution the quadrupole tensor equals tr(I)δij−3Iij, so a body's principal moments fix its far gravitational field (MacCullagh's formula). Torques from the Sun and Moon on Earth's quadrupole cause the precession of the equinoxes, and the same J2 term makes satellite orbits precess.
breaks: Mass is never negative and the mass dipole vanishes about the centre of mass, so the gravitational expansion has no dipole term, unlike the electric case.

name: Phase space and Hamiltonian define the partition function
summary: Gibbs ensembles are probability densities on the canonical phase space of analytical mechanics. The Boltzmann weight exponentiates the Hamiltonian H(q,p), and canonical coordinates fix the invariant counting measure d^{3N}q d^{3N}p/(N! h^{3N}), which gives k_BT/2 to every quadratic term in H.

name: Adiabatic invariants and thermodynamic entropy
summary: Under slow parameter change, the action J = ∮p dq of a periodic orbit is conserved (E/ω for an oscillator). Hertz extended this to the phase-space volume enclosed by the energy shell, so S = k_B ln Φ is unchanged by quasistatic work done without heat: this is the mechanical meaning of a reversible adiabatic process, and it was Ehrenfest's route to old quantum theory.
breaks: Invariance of Φ for many degrees of freedom needs ergodicity on the energy shell; for integrable systems only the individual actions are invariant.

name: Generating functions mirror Maxwell relations
summary: The Legendre transform L → H is the same operation as U(S,V) → F, H, G. Maxwell relations are equal mixed second derivatives of a potential, just as the reciprocity relations of canonical transformations come from a generating function. Both belong to symplectic/contact geometry, in which the equilibrium states of a substance form a Legendre submanifold.
map: p=\tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial q},P=-\tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial Q}\Rightarrow\tfrac{\partial p}{\partial Q}=-\tfrac{\partial P}{\partial q}\ \leftrightarrow\ \left(\tfrac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_S=-\left(\tfrac{\partial P}{\partial S}\right)_V

name: Liouville's theorem makes Gibbs ensembles stationary
summary: Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume, so the Liouville equation accepts any density that depends only on H and the other integrals as a stationary state. That is why microcanonical and canonical densities are equilibria, and why the fine-grained Gibbs entropy is exactly conserved.

name: Jarzynski equality from Hamiltonian dynamics
summary: Jarzynski's original proof takes a system that starts in canonical equilibrium and then evolves under a Hamiltonian H(q,p;λ(t)) driven by an external protocol. The work is the change of H along the trajectory, and Liouville's theorem (volume-preserving flow) turns the average of e^{-βW} into a ratio of partition functions.
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)

name: Onsager–Machlup action and most-probable escape paths
summary: Langevin path probabilities are weighted by an Onsager–Machlup action, which becomes the Freidlin–Wentzell action at weak noise. The most probable transition path therefore solves the Euler–Lagrange (or Hamilton) equations of an auxiliary mechanical problem, and its minimal action reproduces the Arrhenius/Kramers exponent.
map: P[x]\propto e^{-S[x]/D},\ S=\tfrac14\int(\dot x+U'(x))^2dt,\ \min S=\Delta U\Rightarrow r\sim e^{-\Delta U/D}

name: Rigidity percolation and Maxwell constraint counting
summary: Maxwell's count of constraints against degrees of freedom predicts that a central-force spring network becomes rigid at mean coordination z_c = 2d. Under random dilution, the elastic moduli vanish at a rigidity-percolation threshold above the connectivity threshold. This framework is used for network glasses and for jamming of frictionless spheres.

name: 2D melting by dislocation unbinding (KTHNY)
summary: Kosterlitz and Thouless applied defect unbinding to dislocations in 2D crystals. At melting, the renormalized Young's modulus built from the Lamé constants takes the universal value 16π k_BT/a². A hexatic phase follows and melts in turn by disclination unbinding (Halperin–Nelson–Young), a sequence seen in colloidal monolayers.
sources: Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Noisy Burgers equation is the KPZ equation
summary: Setting u = −λ∇h maps the KPZ interface equation exactly onto the stochastically forced Burgers equation, a pressureless Navier–Stokes model. The Cole–Hopf transform linearizes both into a diffusion equation with multiplicative noise (a directed polymer), so the 1D KPZ exponents z = 3/2, α = 1/2 also describe Burgers velocity fluctuations.
sources: Kardar, Parisi & Zhang (1986). "Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 56, 889. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889)

name: Navier–Stokes from Boltzmann (Chapman–Enskog)
summary: Expanding the Boltzmann equation in the Knudsen number (Chapman–Enskog) gives the Euler equations at zeroth order and Navier–Stokes at first order, with the viscosity and heat conductivity computed from the cross-section. The lattice Boltzmann method runs this in reverse: it simulates flows using a discretized BGK collision operator.
sources: Bhatnagar, Gross & Krook (1954). "A Model for Collision Processes in Gases. I. Small Amplitude Processes in Charged and Neutral One-Component Systems". *Phys. Rev.* 94, 511. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.94.511](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.94.511)

name: Green–Kubo viscosity and fluctuating hydrodynamics
summary: The shear viscosity in Navier–Stokes equals the time integral of the equilibrium stress autocorrelation (Green–Kubo). Landau–Lifshitz fluctuating hydrodynamics adds a random stress tensor whose covariance is fixed by η and T through the fluctuation–dissipation theorem.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Amplitude equations as time-dependent Landau theory
summary: Near the onset of Rayleigh–Bénard convection (Ra_c ≈ 1708 for rigid plates), the roll amplitude obeys the Newell–Whitehead–Segel (real Ginzburg–Landau) equation, which has the form of time-dependent Landau theory. Supercritical onset gives A ∝ ε^{1/2}, a coherence length ∝ ε^{-1/2} and a relaxation time ∝ ε^{-1}.
breaks: Pattern-forming systems are driven and usually non-variational (complex Ginzburg–Landau has no free energy). Thermal fluctuations matter only extremely close to onset, where they make the transition weakly first order (Swift–Hohenberg), and the broken symmetry is a spatial pattern with wavenumber selection.
sources: Rayleigh (1916). "On convection currents in a horizontal layer of fluid, when the higher temperature is on the under side". *Phil. Mag.* 32, 529. [doi:10.1080/14786441608635602](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786441608635602)
Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Porous-media flow: percolation's original problem
summary: Broadbent and Hammersley introduced percolation to model fluid passing through a random porous medium (gas-mask filters). The Darcy permeability of Stokes flow through a random medium vanishes at the percolation threshold with the conductivity exponent, and invasion percolation describes slow two-phase displacement at low capillary number.
sources: Broadbent & Hammersley (1957). "Percolation processes: I. Crystals and mazes". *Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc.* 53, 629. [doi:10.1017/S0305004100032680](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100032680)

name: Lorentz reciprocity as Onsager symmetry of Stokes flow
summary: The Lorentz reciprocal theorem makes the resistance and mobility tensors of particles in Stokes flow symmetric; this is the macroscopic face of Onsager reciprocity. Through D_ij = k_BT M_ij they become the symmetric diffusion tensor of Brownian suspensions, and Helmholtz's minimum-dissipation theorem parallels Onsager's least-dissipation principle.
sources: Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)

name: Stokes drag sets Brownian diffusion (Stokes–Einstein)
summary: The low-Reynolds-number drag 6πηa on a sphere is the friction coefficient in the overdamped Langevin equation, and Einstein's relation turns it into the diffusion coefficient. For a micron-sized colloid in water, inertia relaxes in m/γ ~ 0.1 µs, so colloidal Brownian motion happens entirely in the Stokes regime.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 549. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053220806](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053220806)
Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Onset of pipe turbulence is directed percolation
summary: Near the onset of sustained wall-bounded turbulence, turbulent puffs decay and split like active sites in an absorbing-state transition, with laminar flow as the absorbing state (Pomeau's conjecture). Couette and channel experiments in 2016 measured directed-percolation exponents in 1+1 and 2+1 dimensions. In pipe flow, puff decay balances splitting at Re ≈ 2040.
sources: Reynolds (1883). "An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous, and of the law of resistance in parallel channels". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 174, 935. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1883.0029](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1883.0029)

name: Kolmogorov scaling and anomalous exponents
summary: K41 predicts universal inertial-range scaling S_p(r) ∝ (εr)^{p/3}. Measured exponents ζ_p fall below p/3 at large p (intermittency) and behave like anomalous dimensions. The Parisi–Frisch multifractal model obtains them by a Legendre transform, mirroring the free energy–entropy relation.
breaks: Turbulence is a far-from-equilibrium state carrying a constant energy flux, with no free energy and no tunable critical point. Prefactors, unlike ζ_p, depend on the large-scale forcing.
sources: Kolmogorov (1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Renormalization group for randomly stirred fluids
summary: The dynamic RG built for critical dynamics was applied to the randomly forced Navier–Stokes equation (Forster–Nelson–Stephen; Yakhot–Orszag). With a power-law forcing spectrum, the fixed point reproduces Kolmogorov's k^{-5/3} spectrum and estimates the Kolmogorov constant at about 1.6.

breaks: Physical stirring is at large scales, so the expansion parameter needed for K41 is not small. Perturbative RG gives no intermittency corrections; in the Kraichnan passive-scalar model those come from zero modes instead.
sources: Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)

Kolmogorov (1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Virial theorem and negative heat capacity
summary: For bound 1/r systems the virial theorem gives E = −⟨K⟩, so a star or star cluster that loses energy heats up (C < 0). Such states exist in the microcanonical ensemble but not in the canonical one. This is the textbook case of ensemble inequivalence for long-range interactions and the root of the gravothermal catastrophe.

name: Inelastic collisions and granular kinetic theory
summary: Kinetic theory with a restitution coefficient e < 1 describes granular gases. Each collision loses energy, so a homogeneous granular gas cools by Haff's law; the velocity distribution is non-Maxwellian with overpopulated tails, and the homogeneous cooling state is unstable to clustering.

name: Nonlinear dynamics on networks: topology sets thresholds
summary: Spreading, cascade and coupled-unit models are nonlinear dynamical systems on graphs, and network structure fixes where they bifurcate. The heterogeneous mean-field SIS epidemic threshold λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ vanishes on scale-free networks, and the Laplacian eigenvalue ratio decides whether synchronized chaos is stable (the master stability function).
sources: Barabási & Albert (1999). "Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks". *Science* 286, 509. [doi:10.1126/science.286.5439.509](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5439.509)

name: Pitchfork normal form as Landau free-energy flow
summary: The supercritical pitchfork ẋ = μx − x³ is gradient flow on a Landau free energy. Its branches ±√μ give β = 1/2, linear relaxation slows as |μ|^{-1} (critical slowing down, used as an early-warning signal), and the hysteresis of a subcritical pitchfork mirrors a first-order transition.
breaks: A few-variable bifurcation has no thermodynamic limit and no fluctuations, so it is exactly mean-field. Real transitions below the upper critical dimension have non-classical exponents, and Hopf bifurcations have no equilibrium counterpart.

name: Feigenbaum universality as an RG fixed point
summary: Period doubling in smooth unimodal maps is governed by the doubling operator Tg(x) = −αg(g(−x/α)), a renormalization transformation on the space of maps. Its fixed point is universal and δ = 4.6692… is its single relevant eigenvalue, as a thermal eigenvalue sets ν at a Wilson fixed point; the order of the map's maximum plays the role of the universality class.
breaks: The renormalization acts on one-variable maps by functional composition, not on spatial degrees of freedom. There is no free energy or coarse-grained field.
sources: Feigenbaum (1978). "Quantitative universality for a class of nonlinear transformations". *J. Stat. Phys.* 19, 25. [doi:10.1007/BF01020332](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332)

Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)

name: Transition to chaos in random neural networks
summary: Sompolinsky, Crisanti and Sommers solved random recurrent networks with dynamic mean-field theory, a technique taken from spin glasses: at gain g = 1 the quiescent state gives way to chaos with a positive Lyapunov exponent. The same order-to-chaos boundary governs how signals propagate through, and how trainable, deep networks are at initialization.

name: Thermodynamic formalism: Gibbs states of chaotic maps
summary: Sinai, Ruelle and Bowen recast the invariant measures of hyperbolic chaos as Gibbs states of a one-dimensional lattice system on symbol sequences. Topological pressure plays the free energy and sums over periodic orbits play the partition function. Multifractal spectra come from a Legendre transform, the way entropy comes from free energy.
breaks: The 'inverse temperature' β is a formal weighting parameter, not a physical temperature, and the 'lattice' is time along the orbit.
sources: Eckmann & Ruelle (1985). "Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 57, 617. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617)

name: Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy: chaos produces information
summary: The Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy is the Shannon entropy rate of a chaotic trajectory's symbolic sequence. For smooth systems with SRB measures, Pesin's identity equates it to the sum of the positive Lyapunov exponents, so the rate of exponential divergence is the rate at which information about the initial condition is revealed.
sources: Eckmann & Ruelle (1985). "Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 57, 617. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617)
Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)

name: Microscopic chaos and transport coefficients
summary: Boltzmann's molecular-chaos assumption is backed by the strong chaos of hard-sphere and Lorentz gases: Sinai billiards are ergodic and mixing. The Gaspard–Nicolis escape-rate formalism makes this quantitative by writing a diffusion coefficient in terms of the Lyapunov exponents and the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy of the open system's repeller.
breaks: Chaos is sufficient but not necessary for normal transport: some non-chaotic polygonal billiards also diffuse.

name: Fluctuation theorem from thermostatted chaotic dynamics
summary: The first fluctuation theorem (Evans–Cohen–Morriss) and the Gallavotti–Cohen proof both start from deterministic, time-reversible thermostatted dynamics assumed to be chaotic (Anosov). The phase-space contraction rate is identified with entropy production, and the SRB measure takes the place of the Gibbs measure in the steady state.
sources: Evans, Cohen & Morriss (1993). "Probability of second law violations in shearing steady states". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 71, 2401. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2401](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2401)
Eckmann & Ruelle (1985). "Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 57, 617. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.57.617)

name: KAM tori obstruct the ergodic hypothesis
summary: Equilibrium ensembles assume trajectories explore the whole energy shell. KAM theory shows that a positive-measure set of invariant tori survives weak non-integrable perturbations, so time averages need not equal microcanonical averages. Hénon–Heiles made the mixed phase space concrete; the regular fraction shrinks as the perturbation or the number of degrees of freedom grows.
sources: Hénon & Heiles (1964). "The applicability of the third integral of motion: Some numerical experiments". *Astron. J.* 69, 73. [doi:10.1086/109234](https://doi.org/10.1086/109234)

name: Chaotic diffusion in the standard map
summary: Once the last KAM barrier breaks (K ≈ 0.9716), momentum in the Chirikov standard map performs a random walk with a quasilinear diffusion rate, so a deterministic Hamiltonian map behaves like a Fokker–Planck process. Accelerator modes and stickiness near islands make the transport anomalous.

name: Generalized Gibbs ensembles for integrable systems
summary: Integrable systems have extensively many conserved charges, so they relax not to a Gibbs state but to a generalized Gibbs ensemble with one Lagrange multiplier per charge. Generalized hydrodynamics then describes their large-scale flow, and classical soliton gases (KdV, Toda) are a direct mechanical example.

name: Integrability: Lax pairs, Yang–Baxter and Bethe ansatz
summary: Classical inverse scattering, with its Lax pair and infinitely many conserved charges, has the same algebra as transfer-matrix and Bethe-ansatz solvability: commuting families generated by an R-matrix that obeys Yang–Baxter. The quantum inverse scattering method quantizes the classical one. The Lieb–Liniger gas is the quantized nonlinear Schrödinger field, and its attractive bound states are quantum NLS solitons.
sources: Gardner, Greene, Kruskal & Miura (1967). "Method for Solving the Korteweg-deVries Equation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1095. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095)

Lieb & Liniger (1963). "Exact Analysis of an Interacting Bose Gas. I. The General Solution and the Ground State". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 1605. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605)

name: Kuramoto synchronization on complex networks
summary: Phase oscillators coupled along graph edges synchronize at a coupling set by topology. In heterogeneous mean field, K_c is the all-to-all value times ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩, so scale-free hubs make synchrony almost free. Small-world shortcuts, which Watts and Strogatz introduced with coupled oscillators in mind, synchronize far more easily than regular lattices.
sources: Watts & Strogatz (1998). "Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks". *Nature* 393, 440. [doi:10.1038/30918](https://doi.org/10.1038/30918)

Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Kuramoto onset as a mean-field phase transition
summary: The Kuramoto order parameter obeys a self-consistency equation like that of the Curie–Weiss magnet. For a unimodal frequency distribution, synchronization appears continuously at K_c = 2/(πg(0)) with r ∝ (K − K_c)^{1/2}, the mean-field exponent β = 1/2.
breaks: The disorder is in quenched natural frequencies rather than fields, and the dynamics is non-equilibrium, with no free energy for distinct ω_i. With short-range coupling in low dimensions, frequency disorder destroys global phase order, so mean-field behaviour needs long-range coupling.
sources: Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Anderson localization of classical vibrations
summary: Anderson localization is a wave-interference effect, not a specifically quantum one. The normal modes of a mass–spring chain with random masses are exponentially localized, with a localization length that diverges only as ω → 0 where acoustic modes survive. The same physics localizes sound, elastic waves and light in disordered media.
sources: Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

name: FPUT problem: equipartition fails among normal modes
summary: Fermi, Pasta, Ulam and Tsingou expected a weakly anharmonic chain to share energy equally among its normal modes, as equipartition requires. Instead, the energy returned almost entirely to the initial mode. Zabusky and Kruskal traced this recurrence to KdV solitons; today it is read as near-integrability with very long prethermal times.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

name: Phonons: quantized normal modes and heat capacity
summary: Normal-mode analysis turns a harmonic crystal into independent oscillators. Quantized, these become a Bose gas of phonons with zero chemical potential, and the Planck-weighted mode sum gives the Einstein and Debye heat capacities (C ∝ T³ at low T) and the classical Dulong–Petit limit 3Nk_B from equipartition.

name: Damped oscillator: prototype susceptibility and FDT
summary: The driven damped oscillator's χ(ω) is the textbook causal response function: its poles lie in the lower half-plane and it satisfies Kramers–Kronig. The fluctuation–dissipation theorem then fixes its thermal noise spectrum from Im χ, and integrating that spectrum recovers equipartition. This sets the thermal-noise floor of AFM cantilevers, torsion balances and gravitational-wave test masses.
sources: Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)
Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Thermoacoustic engines and refrigerators
summary: A sound wave in a channel with a temperature gradient drives each gas parcel through a Stirling-like cycle of compression, heat exchange with the wall and expansion. Heat can therefore amplify sound (Rijke and Sondhauss tubes, Rayleigh's criterion) or sound can pump heat. Thermoacoustic engines and refrigerators are working heat engines bounded by Carnot.

name: Sound propagation and absorption from kinetic theory
summary: The adiabatic sound speed and the classical Stokes–Kirchhoff absorption both follow from the hydrodynamic limit of the Boltzmann equation, with attenuation set by viscosity and thermal conduction. When ωτ ~ 1, at high frequency or in a rarefied gas, hydrodynamic acoustics breaks down and BGK-type kinetic models describe the sound instead.
sources: Bhatnagar, Gross & Krook (1954). "A Model for Collision Processes in Gases. I. Small Amplitude Processes in Charged and Neutral One-Component Systems". *Phys. Rev.* 94, 511. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.94.511](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.94.511)

name: Kramers escape and stochastic resonance in a double well
summary: Thermal noise drives hops between the wells of a Duffing-type double-well oscillator at the Kramers rate, which depends on the barrier height and the curvatures at the minimum and the saddle. Adding weak periodic forcing produces stochastic resonance: the response peaks when the mean Kramers residence time is about half the drive period.
sources: Kramers (1940). "Brownian Motion in a Field of Force and the Diffusion Model of Chemical Reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)

name: Lagrangian generates quantum propagation (Dirac–Feynman)
summary: Dirac (1933) noticed that the short-time quantum propagator behaves like exp(iS/ħ), with S the classical action. Feynman built the path integral on this, which made the Lagrangian rather than the Hamiltonian the primary object of quantum dynamics.
sources: Feynman (1948). "Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367)

name: Bohmian mechanics as quantum Hamilton–Jacobi theory
summary: With ψ=R e^{iS/ħ}, the Schrödinger equation is exactly a Hamilton–Jacobi equation plus Bohm's quantum potential Q (Madelung 1927, Bohm 1952). De Broglie–Bohm theory has particles move along v=∇S/m, the characteristics of this equation, which gives a deterministic hidden-variable interpretation.
breaks: For many particles Q is nonlocal in configuration space and does not weaken as |ψ| shrinks. The motion is first-order, so initial momenta are not free. The mathematics is exact, but the interpretation is contested.
sources: Bohm (1952). "A Suggested Interpretation of the Quantum Theory in Terms of 'Hidden' Variables. I". *Phys. Rev.* 85, 166. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.85.166](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.85.166)

name: WKB: Schrödinger reduces to Hamilton–Jacobi
summary: Writing ψ=A e^{iS/ħ} turns the Schrödinger equation into the Hamilton–Jacobi equation at leading order, plus a continuity equation for A. Quantizing the action variables J=∮p dq gives the Bohr–Sommerfeld and EBK rules. Ehrenfest argued that action variables were the right quantities to quantize because they are adiabatic invariants.
breaks: It breaks down at turning points and caustics, where A diverges (Airy matching and the Maslov 1/2 repair this), and wherever the de Broglie wavelength changes quickly.
sources: Schrödinger (1926). "Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem". *Ann. Phys.* 384, 361. [doi:10.1002/andp.19263840404](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19263840404)

name: Hannay angle: classical counterpart of the Berry phase
summary: When an integrable system's parameters are cycled adiabatically, the action J stays invariant but the conjugate angle picks up a geometric shift, the Hannay angle. Berry showed that it is the semiclassical limit of the Berry phase of the quantum state with the same quantum number.
breaks: It requires invariant tori. Chaotic systems have no angle variables, and their adiabatic response takes a different form (geometric magnetism, Berry–Robbins).
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: Hamilton's principal function as the semiclassical phase
summary: In the stationary-phase evaluation of the path integral, the phase is Hamilton's principal function S(x_b,x_a,t), which generates the classical time-evolution map. The prefactor is its mixed second derivative (the Van Vleck–Gutzwiller propagator), and caustics of the classical family add Maslov phases.
breaks: It fails near caustics and beyond the Ehrenfest time, where classical paths proliferate (chaos). It also fails where no real classical path exists: tunnelling needs complex or Euclidean paths.

name: Epistemically restricted Liouville mechanics ≈ Gaussian QM
summary: Classical Liouville mechanics with an uncertainty-like limit on what can be known about phase-space points reproduces Gaussian quantum mechanics, including entanglement and teleportation (Bartlett, Rudolph and Spekkens). The genuinely nonclassical resource therefore lies outside it: contextuality, which is equivalent to negativity of the Wigner function.
breaks: The model cannot reproduce non-Gaussian states or operations, Bell violations or Kochen–Specker contextuality, because it is a noncontextual hidden-variable model by construction.

name: Poisson bracket → commutator (canonical quantization)
summary: Dirac recognized that Heisenberg's commutators obey the algebra of classical Poisson brackets, so quantization replaces {A,B} with [Â,B̂]/iħ. Hamilton's equations then become the Heisenberg equations of motion, and the Liouville equation becomes the von Neumann equation for the density matrix.
map: \{A,B\}\to\tfrac{1}{i\hbar}[\hat A,\hat B];\ \dot A=\{A,H\}\to\dot{\hat A}=\tfrac{i}{\hbar}[\hat H,\hat A];\ \partial_t\rho=\{H,\rho\}\to i\hbar\partial_t\hat\rho=[\hat H,\hat\rho]
breaks: The map is not exact for all observables. The Groenewold–van Hove theorem rules out a consistent quantization of all polynomials, so operator ordering is ambiguous at O(ħ²).
sources: Heisenberg (1925). "Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen". *Z. Phys.* 33, 879. [doi:10.1007/BF01328377](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01328377)

name: Phase-space QM: Liouville flow to Wigner–Moyal
summary: The Wigner function is a quasi-probability on classical phase space that evolves by the Liouville equation with the Poisson bracket replaced by the Moyal bracket. Quantum optics describes light with Wigner, Husimi-Q and Glauber–Sudarshan-P distributions; Wigner negativity or a singular P function marks a nonclassical state.
map: \partial_tW=\{H,W\}_{\star}=\{H,W\}+O(\hbar^2\,\partial^3H\,\partial^3W);\ \ W\ \text{follows the classical flow exactly if}\ H\ \text{is quadratic}
breaks: W can be negative, so it is not a probability. Moyal corrections at O(ħ²) appear for anharmonic Hamiltonians, so classical Liouville flow is exact only for quadratic H (linear optics).
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)

name: Circuit quantization from the node-flux Lagrangian
summary: Superconducting circuits are quantized by writing a Lagrangian in node fluxes, with capacitive energy as kinetic energy and inductive and Josephson energy as potential energy. A Legendre transform makes the charges the conjugate momenta, and one then imposes [Φ,Q]=iħ. Kirchhoff loops and flux quantization act as holonomic constraints.
breaks: Dissipative and non-Lagrangian elements (resistors, nonreciprocal gyrators) need a bath or an extended treatment. Offset charges and compact phase variables need care.

name: Least action as stationary phase
summary: As ħ→0, Hamilton's principle δS=0 is the stationary-phase condition of the sum over e^{iS/ħ}: only paths near the classical one interfere constructively, just as Fermat's principle emerges from Huygens' wave optics. In imaginary time the same logic picks out minima of the Euclidean action (instantons).
map: \hbar\to0:\ \int\mathcal{D}x\,e^{iS/\hbar}\ \text{dominated by}\ \delta S=0\ \Leftrightarrow\ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}
sources: Feynman (1948). "Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.20.367)

name: Madelung: condensates as inviscid, irrotational fluids
summary: With ψ=√n e^{iθ}, the Gross–Pitaevskii equation becomes the continuity and Euler equations of an inviscid, irrotational fluid with velocity v=ħ∇θ/m, plus a quantum-pressure term. Kelvin's circulation theorem becomes the topological quantization of circulation around vortex lines, and the Landau criterion sets the critical velocity for dissipation.
map: \mathbf v=\tfrac{\hbar}{m}\nabla\theta;\ \ m\partial_t\mathbf v=-\nabla\big(\tfrac12mv^2+V+gn+Q\big);\ \ \oint\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf l=\tfrac{h}{m}\ell,\ \ell\in\mathbb Z
breaks: The fluid picture fails inside vortex cores and below the healing length ξ, where quantum pressure dominates. At finite temperature a normal component adds viscosity (the two-fluid model).

name: Low-Re swimming as a gauge holonomy (Shapere–Wilczek)
summary: At low Reynolds number, a swimmer's net displacement after a cyclic stroke depends only on the loop traced in shape space: it is the holonomy of a gauge connection, as with the Berry phase. For small strokes the displacement is the curvature times the enclosed area, so reciprocal strokes, which enclose no area, cannot swim (Purcell's scallop theorem).
map: \Delta\mathbf x=\oint_{\rm stroke}\mathcal A(s)\,ds\approx\iint\mathcal F\,da,\ \ \mathcal F=d\mathcal A+\mathcal A\wedge\mathcal A;\ \ \text{reciprocal stroke}\Rightarrow\Delta\mathbf x=0
breaks: The connection is non-abelian (it mixes rotations and translations) and comes from the reciprocity of Stokes flow, not from a quantum state. The effect is purely kinematic and dissipative.
sources: Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Quantum turbulence: Kolmogorov cascades in vortex tangles
summary: Tangles of quantized vortices in superfluid helium and atomic condensates reproduce Kolmogorov's k^{-5/3} spectrum at scales larger than the intervortex spacing. Below that scale, energy moves through vortex reconnections and Kelvin-wave cascades. 2D condensates show inverse cascades and Onsager's negative-temperature vortex clusters.
breaks: There is no viscosity: energy is dissipated by phonon emission and reconnections at the smallest scales. Quantized circulation also imposes a discrete vortex scale that classical turbulence lacks.

name: Kepler–hydrogen: Runge–Lenz vector and hidden SO(4)
summary: The conserved Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector, which keeps Kepler orbits closed (Bertrand's theorem), enlarges the symmetry of the 1/r problem from SO(3) to SO(4). Pauli (1926) used its quantum version to derive the hydrogen spectrum algebraically, and the same symmetry explains hydrogen's accidental n² degeneracy.
map: \mathbf A=\mathbf p\times\mathbf L-mk\,\hat{\mathbf r};\ \ \mathfrak{so}(4):\ E_n=-\frac{mk^2}{2\hbar^2n^2},\ g_n=n^2\ \ (k=Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0)
breaks: Any departure from 1/r (relativity, core penetration, spin–orbit coupling) breaks SO(4). Classically the orbits then precess; quantum mechanically the ℓ-levels split.

name: Rutherford scattering: classical = quantum for 1/r
summary: The Coulomb differential cross section comes out the same from classical orbits, from the first Born approximation and from the exact quantum solution. This accident of the 1/r potential is why Rutherford's classical analysis could reveal the nucleus. For other potentials, features of the classical deflection function (rainbows, glories, orbiting) reappear as stationary-phase points of the partial-wave sum (Ford–Wheeler).
breaks: In general the classical and quantum cross sections differ. Diffraction and shadow scattering make the quantum total cross section of a hard sphere twice its geometric value at high energy, and identical-particle (Mott) interference has no classical analogue.
sources: Born (1926). "Zur Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge". *Z. Phys.* 37, 863. [doi:10.1007/BF01397477](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01397477)

name: Symplectic splitting ↔ Trotter–Suzuki Hamiltonian simulation
summary: Long-term N-body integration splits H into exactly solvable flows (leapfrog, Wisdom–Holman, Yoshida–Suzuki compositions). Digital quantum simulation uses the same product formulas for e^{-iHt}. The error is set by nested Poisson brackets in the classical case and nested commutators in the quantum case.
breaks: Classical integrators preserve symplecticity, which keeps the energy error bounded; quantum product formulas are exactly unitary. Quantum cost is counted in gates, and the error scales with commutator norms.

name: Ehrenfest theorem: Newton's second law on average
summary: Expectation values obey m d²⟨x⟩/dt² = −⟨V′(x)⟩, Newton's second law for the centroid of a wave packet. The centroid follows the classical trajectory only when ⟨V′(x)⟩=V′(⟨x⟩): for at most quadratic potentials, or for packets narrow compared with the scale over which the force changes.
map: m\frac{d^2\langle\hat x\rangle}{dt^2}=-\langle V'(\hat x)\rangle\approx-V'(\langle\hat x\rangle)\ \ (\text{exact iff}\ V'''=0)
breaks: Wave-packet spreading and anharmonicity spoil the agreement after the Ehrenfest time. The theorem does not imply classical behaviour of individual measurement outcomes.

name: Atom interferometers as gravimeters and Sagnac gyroscopes
summary: Light-pulse atom interferometers turn the classical kinematics of free fall and rotating frames into matter-wave phases. The gravity phase k_eff g T² underlies atomic gravimeters, and the Sagnac phase from Earth's rotation makes atom gyroscopes; when rotation is not the target, the Coriolis terms must be compensated.
breaks: For equal area, the matter-wave Sagnac phase exceeds the optical one by mc²/ħω ~ 10^10, but atom interferometers enclose far smaller areas.

name: Rotation as synthetic magnetism: Coriolis ↔ Lorentz
summary: In a frame rotating at Ω the Coriolis force has the form of a Lorentz force with qB=2mΩ. Rotating condensates therefore form triangular vortex lattices, like type-II superconductors in a field, and as Ω approaches the trap frequency they enter the lowest-Landau-level regime, which resembles the quantum Hall effect.
breaks: The centrifugal term weakens confinement and frees the gas as Ω→ω⊥, which has so far kept rotating gases out of deep fractional-quantum-Hall states. Laser-induced gauge fields avoid this problem.
sources: Bloch, Dalibard & Zwerger (2008). "Many-body physics with ultracold gases". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 80, 885. [arXiv:0704.3011](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.3011)

name: Foucault pendulum precession as a holonomy
summary: After one sidereal day, the Foucault pendulum's plane of swing has turned by the solid angle enclosed by its circle of latitude, a holonomy of parallel transport on a sphere. The same geometry gives a spin's Berry phase as −m times the solid angle traced by the field direction.
breaks: Foucault's pendulum transports a real vector (an SO(2) holonomy of the sphere's Levi-Civita connection). Berry's phase is a U(1) phase of a complex state; it scales with m and shows up only relative to another path.
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: BGS conjecture: classical chaos ↔ random-matrix spectra
summary: Whether the classical limit is integrable or chaotic fixes the quantum level statistics: Poisson spacings for integrable motion (Berry–Tabor), Wigner–Dyson level repulsion for fully chaotic motion (Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit), and intermediate statistics for mixed KAM phase spaces. Periodic-orbit theory explains why.
map: P_{\rm int}(s)=e^{-s}\ \ \text{vs}\ \ P_{\rm GOE}(s)\approx\frac{\pi s}{2}e^{-\pi s^2/4}
breaks: There are exceptions. Arithmetic chaotic systems, such as billiards on special constant-curvature surfaces, show Poisson statistics, and non-generic integrable systems such as harmonic oscillators do not follow Berry–Tabor.
sources: Bohigas, Giannoni & Schmit (1984). "Characterization of Chaotic Quantum Spectra and Universality of Level Fluctuation Laws". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 52, 1. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.1)

name: Bosonic Josephson junction: pendulum bifurcation, self-trapping
summary: The mean-field dynamics of a condensate in a double well, in population imbalance z and relative phase φ, is that of a nonrigid pendulum. Raising the interaction parameter Λ through a bifurcation produces macroscopic quantum self-trapping, observed with rubidium in 2005; the large atom number N plays the role of 1/ħ.
breaks: At finite N, quantum fluctuations cause collapse and revival and tunnelling between the two self-trapped states. The classical pendulum is only the N→∞ limit.

name: Period doubling vs discrete time-crystalline order
summary: Driven dissipative classical systems (Faraday waves, parametrically driven pendula, period-doubling bifurcations) respond robustly at twice the drive period. Discrete time crystals are the many-body quantum version: a period-doubled response that resists drive imperfections and is long-range ordered, seen in trapped ions, NV centres and superconducting processors.
breaks: Classical period doubling relies on dissipation into an attractor. Closed quantum time crystals must avoid Floquet heating through many-body localization or prethermalization, and their rigidity is a many-body effect, although classical many-body time crystals in coupled dissipative oscillators have been proposed.

name: Chaos, Ehrenfest time and decoherence
summary: Classical chaos stretches a wave packet exponentially, so an isolated chaotic system stops tracking its classical counterpart after the Ehrenfest time, ~λ⁻¹ln(S/ħ), which for Saturn's moon Hyperion is only decades. Environmental decoherence restores the classical Liouville limit. Zurek and Paz argued that the entropy production rate then becomes independent of ħ and is set by the Lyapunov exponents.
breaks: Entropy production at the Lyapunov rate holds in an intermediate range of decoherence strength and is supported numerically, not proven in general.
sources: Zurek (2003). "Decoherence, einselection, and the quantum origins of the classical". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 715. [arXiv:quant-ph/0105127](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0105127)

name: Lyapunov exponent ↔ OTOC growth and the chaos bound
summary: The out-of-time-order correlator is the quantum version of the squared Poisson bracket {x(t),p}², which measures sensitivity to initial conditions. In semiclassical systems it therefore grows as e^{2λt}, with λ the classical Lyapunov exponent, until the scrambling time. Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford bounded the quantum rate by 2πk_BT/ħ.
breaks: Exponential OTOC growth lasts only until t~λ⁻¹ln(1/ħ_eff). It is absent in many chaotic systems with small local Hilbert spaces (spin-1/2 chains), and unstable saddle points in integrable systems produce it without chaos. The thermal bound has no classical counterpart.
sources: Maldacena, Shenker & Stanford (2016). "A bound on chaos". *JHEP* 08, 106. [arXiv:1503.01409](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01409)

name: Ergodicity: classical mixing vs eigenstate thermalization
summary: Classical statistical mechanics rests on chaotic, mixing motion on the energy shell. Its quantum replacement, the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, holds that individual eigenstates of chaotic Hamiltonians already look thermal; Srednicki derived it from Berry's random-wave conjecture for the eigenfunctions of classically chaotic systems.
breaks: ETH concerns eigenstates, not trajectories, and does not need a classical limit (spin-1/2 chains obey it). Many-body localization and quantum many-body scars, named after Heller's periodic-orbit scars, violate it.
sources: Deutsch (1991). "Quantum statistical mechanics in a closed system". *Phys. Rev. A* 43, 2046. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.43.2046](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.43.2046)
Srednicki (1994). "Chaos and quantum thermalization". *Phys. Rev. E* 50, 888. [arXiv:cond-mat/9403051](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9403051)

name: Kicked rotor: chaotic diffusion vs dynamical localization
summary: Chirikov's standard map loses its last KAM torus near K≈0.97, after which momentum diffuses without bound. The quantum kicked rotor follows this diffusion only up to a break time and then localizes in momentum. Fishman, Grempel and Prange mapped this dynamical localization onto Anderson localization, and it was observed with cold atoms in pulsed optical standing waves.
map: p_{n+1}=p_n+K\sin\theta_n,\ \ \theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+p_{n+1};\ \ \langle p^2\rangle_{\rm cl}\approx\tfrac{K^2}{2}n\ \ \text{vs quantum saturation after}\ t^*\propto D/\hbar_{\rm eff}^2
breaks: Localization is a quantum interference effect with no classical counterpart. Noise or decoherence restores classical diffusion, and at quantum resonances (rational ħ_eff/4π) the energy grows ballistically.

name: Torus quantization (EBK) and Gutzwiller's periodic-orbit sum
summary: Einstein (1917) quantized the actions on invariant tori and noted that the rule fails when the tori are destroyed. KAM theory says which tori survive. For fully chaotic motion, Gutzwiller's trace formula, a stationary-phase evaluation of the path integral, replaces torus quantization with a sum over unstable periodic orbits.
breaks: Mixed phase spaces need both pictures, plus tunnelling between regular and chaotic regions. The periodic-orbit sum diverges because the number of orbits grows exponentially, so it has to be resummed.

name: Gross–Pitaevskii = NLS: matter-wave solitons
summary: In a 1D waveguide the Gross–Pitaevskii equation reduces to the integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Repulsive condensates therefore carry dark solitons and attractive ones bright solitons and soliton trains, all seen in BECs between 1999 and 2002. The same equation governs solitons in optical fibres.
breaks: Transverse confinement and the trap break integrability. In 2D and 3D, dark solitons decay into vortices through the snake instability, and attractive 3D condensates collapse. Beyond mean field, the quantum NLS (Lieb–Liniger) is solved by the Bethe ansatz.

name: Integrability blocks thermalization: Lax charges and GGE
summary: Classical integrable systems carry an extensive set of conserved quantities generated by a Lax pair. That is why soliton collisions are elastic and FPUT-type lattices recur instead of equilibrating. Quantum integrable systems (Lieb–Liniger, the quantum NLS) likewise fail to thermalize and relax to a generalized Gibbs ensemble, as the quantum Newton's cradle experiment showed.
breaks: Quantum conserved charges constrain relaxation only if they are local or quasi-local. In both the classical and quantum cases, weak integrability breaking gives prethermal plateaus and eventually thermalization.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

name: Harmonic oscillator: normal modes to ladder operators
summary: Any small oscillation about equilibrium, once reduced to normal modes, quantizes to the quantum harmonic oscillator. The classical complex amplitude becomes the ladder operator a, giving the equally spaced spectrum ħω(n+1/2) that is the template for phonons, photons and quasiparticles.
breaks: The zero-point energy ħω/2 and the discrete exchange of energy have no classical counterpart. The equal level spacing is why the classical and quantum frequencies coincide.

name: Bogoliubov transformation: normal modes of a condensate
summary: Linearizing about the condensate gives a quadratic bosonic Hamiltonian that a Bogoliubov transformation diagonalizes. This is normal-mode analysis with a symplectic rather than orthogonal transformation, and it yields phonon-like quasiparticles. In traps, the low-lying collective modes (the Kohn dipole mode at the trap frequency, breathing and quadrupole modes) are measured like classical normal modes.
breaks: Classical normal-mode analysis has no counterpart to the u,v mixing of creation and annihilation operators, which produces quantum depletion and a two-mode-squeezed ground state.
